theme_scores.justification: The objective (MSY, EU obligations, Biodiversity 2020) is clearly stated and linked to the mechanism (national ban), but these claims carry no citations at all.
Alternatives (IFCA byelaws, seasonal ban, do nothing) are explained with clear reasoning for rejection, and some claims cite MMO FAD (Reference 2) and STECF (Reference 3), giving a traceable source.
The v-notching scheme's insufficient uptake is evidenced with Cefas portside sampling showing berried lobsters are ~14% of landings, linked to Reference 1 and 13 (SI 2000).

Detailed cost estimates (£2.36m, £35.9m) are built from cited MMO/Seafish/ONS data (References 1,2,16,17,21-23), with explicit acknowledgment of assumptions, uncertainty and a low-cost sensitivity scenario, showing the document assessing its own evidence base.

The Cefas dynamic population model (References 8,9) is described in detail with two scenarios, uncertainty ranges (3-43%), and explicit caveats that results are illustrative and not tied to specific functional units, demonstrating self-assessment of the evidence.

Key assumptions about compliance and IFCA overlaps are explained and linked to Reference 5 (Marine and Coastal Access Act) and Reference 1, though weaknesses are noted but not deeply assessed for uncertainty.

The document explicitly flags a data gap (North-West functional unit lacking berried-proportion evidence, Reference 3) and explains how this limitation affected the calculations, an example of assessing the evidence base's weaknesses.
Claims about Landing Obligation exemptions and the EU technical measures proposal are asserted with no citations, only narrative explanation.
Numeric net benefit figures are given but with no citations or methodological linkage in this theme's text alone.
The 3-43% landings benefit is mentioned again but without citation in this theme's text.
Claims about reduced enforcement issues and resource intensity are asserted without citation.
Restates cost and benefit figures (£35.9m, £2.29m, 3-43%) without new citations in this theme, relying on evidence detailed elsewhere.

reasoning: The document shows a reasonably strong evidence trail for its core cost-benefit case: MMO landings data, Cefas sampling and a dynamic population model are cited (References 1, 2, 3, 8, 9) and the document explicitly discusses assumptions, sensitivities (the low-cost scenario reducing costs to £2.25m) and uncertainties (e.g. 'It is uncertain how well this general lobster population corresponds to each of the individual functional units'). This meets Level 3 criteria for the cost and benefit sections specifically. However, the rationale for the intervention itself -- why a national ban meets MSY/EU obligations, why voluntary v-notching failed, and the EU Landing Obligation context -- often rests on uncited assertions ('For England, the policy objective is to improve stock health...' has no reference; the EU Landing Obligation exclusion of lobsters is asserted without citation). The strongest counter-example against Level 3 overall is that the foundational policy objective and the options analysis, while logically argued, are not linked to named sources as rigorously as the cost/benefit modelling is -- many objective-related sentences carry empty <references> blocks. Because the rubric requires that the assessed level hold across most of what the document should explain, not just the cost/benefit calculations, the weaker sourcing on rationale, EU context and implementation drags the overall score down. To reach a full Level 3 across the whole section, the document would need to cite and assess evidence behind the policy rationale and EU/international claims with the same rigor shown in the cost and stock-modelling analysis.
